fetched_contents.text: Review and Comparative Analysis of Databases for Speech Emotion Recognition 1. Introduction Human beings can express emotions in multidimensional ways. Among these, the most commonly used methods are facial expressions, speech, body language, gestures, and writing [1]. In recent times, several systems have been developed to identify emotions from speech signals. Still, classical automatic speech recognition systems have not paid much attention to paralinguistic information of the speech, like gender, emotion and personality. However, paralinguistic data is relevant for efficient communication and to understand one another. Speech emotion recognition (SER) is therefore considered with growing interest in investigating emotional states through speech signals. The ability to recognize emotions has the potential to significantly enhance human–computer interaction (HCI), making it more intuitive and responsive to users’ emotional states [2]. SER has diverse applications across various domains, including robotics, mobile services, and call centers. For example, in [3], the authors propose a new model of SER based on deep neural networks to improve the human–robot interaction. Instead, in [4], the authors developed a smartphone application powered by cloud computing that identifies emotions in real time using a standard speech corpus. Furthermore, in [5], the authors propose a call redistribution method based on SER that shows a remarkable reduction in waiting time for more urgent callers. More recently, the applications of SER have expanded across healthcare, customer service, HCI and psychological assessment [6,7]. For instance, the integration of SER into smart home technologies and mental health monitoring systems highlights its potential in monitoring emotional well-being, particularly in personalized healthcare contexts [8]. Since affective disorders are associated with specific voice patterns, in [9], the authors explored a generalizable approach to evaluate clinical depression and remission from voice using transfer learning. They found that the SER model was able to accurately identify the presence of depression, providing a successful method for early diagnosis. Despite its wide range of applications, SER remains a challenging task. Emotions vary not only between individuals but also across cultures and contexts, and their acoustic expression often overlaps across categories. Variability in recording conditions, imbalance in class distributions, and the difficulty of capturing spontaneous affect further complicate system design. Among these issues, the question of how emotions are represented and annotated in data is particularly critical: the lack of consensus on categorization schemes and the inherent subjectivity of labeling make it difficult to build consistent training corpora. Several key databases have therefore emerged in SER research, each addressing these challenges in different ways and serving distinct purposes depending on the type of emotional speech being studied. Speech corpora used in SER are collected under various conditions, ranging from controlled laboratory settings with scripted speech to spontaneous, real-world interactions. The selection of speech types significantly impacts the training and performance of SER systems, as the variability in emotional expression across different contexts and datasets poses challenges in building models that generalize well [10,11]. Choosing the right dataset, therefore, plays a decisive role in the design and performance of SER systems, shaping their ability to generalize across speakers, maintain reliable annotations, and adapt to cultural differences. Although SER has been the subject of numerous surveys, most of them concentrate on features, models, and performance comparisons rather than the databases themselves. When datasets are mentioned, they are usually reduced to compact tables listing the language, number of speakers, or targeted emotions, and the most recent reviews include corpora only up to 2021 [12,13]. To the best of our knowledge, no dedicated review has yet examined emotional speech corpora in their own right, how they are collected, the contexts they represent, and the challenges they introduce for system design. This is the gap our paper aims to address. To the best of our knowledge, we provide a broad and up-to-date comparative review of emotional speech databases up to mid-2025, combining both technical and psychological perspectives. Rather than aiming for exhaustiveness, our selection balances historical “pillar” corpora (e.g., DES, SUSAS, EMO-DB), widely used benchmarks (e.g., IEMOCAP, AIBO), linguistically and culturally diverse resources (e.g., CASIA Mandarin, ITA-DB, INTERFACE), and more recent or domain-specific datasets, such as those built from stress speech or emergency calls. We also include innovative corpora that introduced new methodologies or collection processes, setting precedents for subsequent work in the field. fetched_contents.text: DrawSpeech: Expressive Speech Synthesis Using Prosodic Sketches as Control Conditions This project is partially supported by the General Research Fund from the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong SAR Government (Project No. 14202623). Shan Yang Tencent AI Lab Shenzhen, China shaanyang@tencent.com Guangzhi Li {@IEEEauthorhalign} Xixin Wu Tencent AI Lab Shenzhen, China guangzhilei@tencent.com The Chinese University of Hong Kong Hong Kong SAR, China wuxx@se.cuhk.edu.hk Abstract Controlling text-to-speech (TTS) systems to synthesize speech with the prosodic characteristics expected by users has attracted much attention. To achieve controllability, current studies focus on two main directions: (1) using reference speech as prosody prompt to guide speech synthesis, and (2) using natural language descriptions to control the generation process. However, finding reference speech that exactly contains the prosody that users want to synthesize takes a lot of effort. Description-based guidance in TTS systems can only determine the overall prosody, which has difficulty in achieving fine-grained prosody control over the synthesized speech. In this paper, we propose DrawSpeech, a sketch-conditioned diffusion model capable of generating speech based on any prosody sketches drawn by users. Specifically, the prosody sketches are fed to DrawSpeech to provide a rough indication of the expected prosody trends. DrawSpeech then recovers the detailed pitch and energy contours based on the coarse sketches and synthesizes the desired speech. Experimental results show that DrawSpeech can generate speech with a wide variety of prosody and can precisely control the fine-grained prosody in a user-friendly manner. Our implementation and audio samples are publicly available111https://happycolor.github.io/DrawSpeech. Index Terms: Speech Synthesis, Prosody Control, Sketch I Introduction Given a piece of text, we can express it through various prosodic patterns, each conveying distinct meanings [1]. For example, in the same sentence, speakers may emphasize different words to highlight specific information, leading to entirely different interpretations [2]. Thus, controlling a text-to-speech (TTS) system to synthesize the exact prosody desired by users has attracted considerable attention from researchers [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Current research on prosody-controllable TTS systems has explored two primary directions. One approach involves selecting a reference speech as a prosody prompt and instructing the TTS model to replicate the prosodic pattern on the target text [9, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. Typically, StyleTTS [10] extracted a style vector from the reference speech and adopted a prosody predictor to predict pitch and energy based on the extracted style vector. NaturalSpeech 3 [11] disentangled prosody attributes from the reference speech, which then served as prosody condition for a prosody diffusion model to generate prosody representations for the input text. However, finding a reference speech that precisely matches the desired prosody pattern can be time-consuming [16]. In addition, transferring the prosody from the reference speech results in reduced prosodic variations [17]. Another mainstream approach for controlling synthesized prosody is to use natural language descriptions to specify the desired prosody [18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25]. For example, PromptStyle [20] aligns the description prompt embedding with the style embedding during training, enabling description-based control during inference. Mini-report on simulated expressive speech data collection

Lab-generated or simulated expressive speech data typically includes controlled speech with explicitly designed prosody, emotional tone, and expressive variations that can be manipulated or annotated afterward. The evidence points to methods for recording such corpora, including scripted or lab-generated speech, and notes that simulated or expressive speech datasets are often used to study emotion recognition and other paralinguistic tasks [N1-R3]. In the synthesis context, simulated expressive speech is used to train systems that can control prosody and emotion, such as through sketch-based control or reference-based prompting [N3-F3]. One specific example is the EXPRESSO dataset, which contains both expressive read speech and improvised dialogues across multiple styles performed by a small number of speakers [N3-R4].

Common collection protocols and stimulus design for simulated data tend to involve structured stimulus sets and controlled conditions. The reviewed comparative analysis of speech databases describes datasets collected under various conditions, ranging from controlled laboratory settings with scripted speech to spontaneous, real-world interactions [N1-F1]. In practice, simulated expressive speech data collection often uses lab-generated or scripted stimuli, with the goal of producing repeatable and controllable speech samples that can be annotated for prosody, emotion, or other features. The same review emphasizes that databases used in SER research are collected under various conditions and that the selection of speech types significantly impacts training and performance [N1-F1].

Annotations or ground truth are obtained through careful labeling of the collected speech. The review notes that a critical issue in SER is the lack of consensus on categorization schemes and the inherent subjectivity of labeling, making it difficult to build consistent training corpora [N1-F1]. In the synthesis context, ground truth is needed for prosody control: DrawSpeech and related work show that users must provide a rough prosody sketch, and the model then recovers detailed pitch and energy contours from that sketch [N3-F3]. The evidence also implies that simulated data are often annotated for prosody and emotion because they are used to train controllable speech synthesis systems [N3-R3], [N3-R5]. Overall, simulated expressive speech data collection combines lab-controlled stimuli, scripted or expressive read speech, and reference-based or sketch-based design, with annotations obtained by labeling prosody and emotion in ways that support controllable synthesis [N1-F1], [N3-F3], [N3-R4].

Mini-report on spontaneous expressive speech data collection

Spontaneous expressive speech data typically includes naturally occurring conversational speech with rich prosody, emotional cues, and pragmatic variation. The evidence shows that spontaneous speech datasets such as SSSD and CASPER collect conversations between participants and emphasize natural, unscripted dialogue [N2-F2], [N2-R3]. The same evidence notes that spontaneous speech has many affective and pragmatic functions and that spontaneous speech often contains reduced articulation, fillers, repetitions, and other disfluencies, which make the text and acoustics less aligned than in read speech [N4-F4]. This is important because spontaneous expressive speech is not merely “natural” speech; it includes the expressive phenomena that are especially relevant to expressive speech synthesis.

Common collection settings for spontaneous expressive speech are conversational, often involving two-party interactions and crowdsourced or distributed recording. The SSSD paper describes a crowdsourcing approach using Amazon Mechanical Turk, where anonymous participants are randomly paired for unscripted voice conversations, and the dataset features conversations averaging 25–30 minutes across a wide range of everyday topics [N2-F2]. The SSSD methodology also includes a qualification round to select reliable workers and a main recording structure for live two-person sessions, highlighting the logistical challenges of live interaction [N2-F2]. The evidence also points to other large-scale spontaneous speech datasets such as CASPER, which release Stage 1 data with over 200 hours of spontaneous speech [N2-R3], and to broader spontaneous conversational corpora such as Switchboard and Fisher, which are mentioned as telephone-based corpora with important but limited settings [N2-F2]. These settings are important because they reflect the goal of capturing ecologically valid speech rather than highly controlled read speech.

Speaker-task designs in spontaneous expressive speech collection are usually open-ended or topic-starting, with participants allowed to deviate freely from the initial prompt. SSSD provides predefined topics as conversation starters, but participants are allowed to deviate freely, resulting in broader and more natural conversations [N2-F2]. This design is consistent with the broader literature on spontaneous conversation, where the aim is to capture natural, spontaneous interaction rather than rigidly scripted exchanges [N2-R2]. The evidence also suggests that spontaneous speech is often collected in real-world or near-real-world settings, such as crowdsourced platforms or live interactive environments [N2-F2], [N2-R5]. This makes the data more ecologically valid but also more difficult to control and annotate.

Spontaneous data is cleaned and annotated through quality control and labeling processes. The SSSD paper explicitly describes a two-tiered task structure: a qualification round to select reliable workers, followed by main recording sessions [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that spontaneous speech datasets are compared against other datasets, and analyses of conversational content and speech quality are presented [N2-F2]. In the broader context, the review on speech emotion recognition emphasizes that spontaneous speech is difficult to annotate consistently due to variability in recording conditions, imbalance in class distributions, and the difficulty of capturing spontaneous affect [N1-F1]. For spontaneous expressive speech, annotation is therefore likely to focus on prosody, emotion, and conversational phenomena such as turn-taking, disfluencies, and pragmatic cues [N4-F4]. The result is that spontaneous data is cleaned through quality checks and annotated with the same kinds of labels used in SER research, but the process is more challenging because of the natural variability and less structured nature of the speech [N1-F1], [N2-F2].

Mini-report on synthesis applications and use cases

Simulated speech data are used primarily in tasks that require controllable prosody, emotion, and expressive synthesis. The evidence shows that simulated expressive speech is used to train systems that can control prosody and emotion, such as through sketch-based control or reference-based prompting [N3-F3]. DrawSpeech is an example of a simulated-data-oriented synthesis system that conditions on prosody sketches to generate speech with varied prosody and fine-grained control [N3-F3]. The same evidence also notes that modern TTS systems are often trained on vast datasets encompassing diverse speakers, styles, and conditions, and that expressive speech synthesis is increasingly focused on controllability [N3-R2], [N3-R3]. In other words, simulated speech data support tasks such as zero-shot style and prosody control, expressive speech synthesis, and controllable TTS, where the goal is to synthesize speech with desired prosodic and emotional properties rather than simply reproduce read speech [N3-R2], [N3-R5].

Spontaneous speech data are used in tasks that require ecological validity, expressive realism, and modeling of natural conversational phenomena. The evidence highlights that spontaneous speech has many affective and pragmatic functions and that spontaneous speech datasets are used to study real-world interaction and expressive phenomena [N4-F4]. The SSSD paper describes spontaneous two-party conversations and emphasizes longer conversations averaging 25–30 minutes, which allows study of discourse phenomena over extended periods [N2-F2]. In the synthesis context, spontaneous speech is particularly useful for prosody-controllable spontaneous TTS and for synthesizing expressive phenomena such as creaky voice [N4-F4]. The evidence also indicates that spontaneous speech is used to train systems that can handle reduced articulation, fillers, repetitions, and other disfluencies, which are common in natural speech but less present in read speech [N4-F4]. This makes spontaneous data especially relevant for dialogue systems, speech synthesis, and speech recognition, where the goal is to model naturally occurring speech rather than highly controlled read speech [N2-F2].

Each data type supports different synthesis goals. Simulated data support controllability and fine-grained prosody/emotion control because they are more easily manipulated and annotated [N3-F3], [N3-R3]. They are well suited for training systems that can generate speech with desired prosody sketches, reference-style prompting, or explicit emotion control signals [N3-F3], [N3-R2]. In contrast, spontaneous data support ecological validity and expressive realism because they capture natural speech phenomena, disfluencies, and conversational pragmatics [N2-F2], [N4-F4]. They are better suited for tasks requiring natural-sounding speech, dialogue modeling, and the synthesis of expressive phenomena that are difficult to replicate in read speech [N4-F4]. The evidence also notes that simulated data can be generated in large quantities and are easier to collect than spontaneous data, while spontaneous data are harder to annotate and require more careful quality control [N5-R1], [N1-F1]. Overall, simulated data are used when the priority is controllability and reproducibility, while spontaneous data are used when the priority is realism and ecological validity [N3-R3], [N4-F4], [N5-R1].

The branch reports collectively show a clear tradeoff between **simulated** and **spontaneous expressive speech data**:

In short, simulated data are the workhorse for **controllability**, while spontaneous data are the workhorse for **realism**. The best expressive speech synthesis systems often combine both types of data: simulated data for controlled synthesis and spontaneous data for ecological validity [N3-R3], [N4-F4], [N5-R1].

Spontaneous expressive speech data typically includes naturally occurring conversational speech with rich prosody, emotional cues, and pragmatic variation. The evidence shows that spontaneous speech datasets such as SSSD and CASPER collect conversations between participants and emphasize natural, unscripted dialogue [N2-F2], [N2-R3]. The same evidence notes that spontaneous speech has many affective and pragmatic functions and that spontaneous speech often contains reduced articulation, fillers, repetitions, and other disfluencies, which make the text and acoustics less aligned than in read speech [N4-F4]. This is important because spontaneous expressive speech is not merely “natural” speech; it includes the expressive phenomena that are especially relevant to expressive speech synthesis.

Common collection settings for spontaneous expressive speech are conversational, often involving two-party interactions and crowdsourced or distributed recording. The SSSD paper describes a crowdsourcing approach using Amazon Mechanical Turk, where anonymous participants are randomly paired for unscripted voice conversations, and the dataset features conversations averaging 25–30 minutes across a wide range of everyday topics [N2-F2]. The SSSD methodology also includes a qualification round to select reliable workers and a main recording structure for live two-person sessions, highlighting the logistical challenges of live interaction [N2-F2]. Speaker-task designs in spontaneous expressive speech collection are usually open-ended or topic-starting, with participants allowed to deviate freely from the initial prompt. SSSD provides predefined topics as conversation starters, but participants are allowed to deviate freely, resulting in broader and more natural conversations [N2-F2]. This design is consistent with the broader literature on spontaneous conversation, where the aim is to capture natural, spontaneous interaction rather than rigidly scripted exchanges [N2-R2]. The evidence also suggests that spontaneous speech is often collected in real-world or near-real-world settings, such as crowdsourced platforms or live interactive environments [N2-F2], [N2-R5]. Spontaneous data is cleaned and annotated through quality control and labeling processes. The same evidence notes that spontaneous speech has many affective and pragmatic functions and that spontaneous speech often contains reduced articulation, fillers, repetitions, and other disfluencies, which make the text and acoustics less aligned than in read speech [N4-F4]. This is important because spontaneous expressive speech is not merely “natural” speech; it includes the expressive phenomena that are especially relevant to expressive speech synthesis.

Common collection settings for spontaneous expressive speech are conversational, often involving two-party interactions and crowdsourced or distributed recording. The SSSD paper describes a crowdsourcing approach using Amazon Mechanical Turk, where anonymous participants are randomly paired for unscripted voice conversations, and the dataset features conversations averaging 25–30 minutes across a wide range of everyday topics [N2-F2]. The SSSD methodology also includes a qualification round to select reliable workers and a main recording structure for live two-person sessions, highlighting the logistical challenges of live interaction [N2-F2]. Speaker-task designs in spontaneous expressive speech collection are usually open-ended or topic-starting, with participants allowed to deviate freely from the initial prompt. SSSD provides predefined topics as conversation starters, but participants are allowed to deviate freely, resulting in broader and more natural conversations [N2-F2]. This design is consistent with the broader literature on spontaneous conversation, where the aim is to capture natural interaction rather than rigidly scripted exchanges [N2-R2]. The evidence also suggests that spontaneous speech is often collected in **real-world or near-real-world settings**, such as crowdsourced platforms or live interactive environments [N2-F2], [N2-R5].

### How spontaneous data is cleaned and annotated
Spontaneous data are cleaned and annotated through **quality control and labeling processes**. The SSSD paper explicitly describes a two-tiered task structure: a qualification round to select reliable workers, followed by main recording sessions [N2-F2]. The branch report also notes that spontaneous speech datasets are compared against other datasets, and analyses of conversational content and speech quality are presented [N2-F2]. In the broader context, the review on speech emotion recognition emphasizes that spontaneous speech is difficult to annotate consistently due to variability in recording conditions, imbalance in class distributions, and the difficulty of capturing spontaneous affect [N1-F1]. For spontaneous expressive speech, annotation is therefore likely to focus on prosody, emotion, and conversational phenomena such as turn-taking, disfluencies, and pragmatic cues [N4-F4].

## 3. How each data type is used in expressive speech synthesis

### Tasks using simulated speech data
Simulated speech data are used primarily in tasks that require **controllable prosody, emotion, and expressive synthesis**. The branch report says simulated expressive speech is used to train systems that can control prosody and emotion, such as through sketch-based control or reference-based prompting [N3-F3]. DrawSpeech is an example of a simulated-data-oriented synthesis system that conditions on prosody sketches to generate speech with varied prosody and fine-grained control [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that modern TTS systems are often trained on vast datasets encompassing diverse speakers, styles, and conditions, and that expressive speech synthesis is increasingly focused on controllability [N3-R2], [N3-R3]. In other words, simulated speech data support tasks such as **zero-shot style and prosody control**, **expressive speech synthesis**, and **controllable TTS**, where the goal is to synthesize speech with desired prosodic and emotional properties rather than simply reproduce read speech [N3-R2], [N3-R5].

### Tasks using spontaneous speech data
Spontaneous speech data are used in tasks that require **ecological validity, expressive realism, and modeling of natural conversational phenomena**. The branch report notes that spontaneous speech has many affective and pragmatic functions and that spontaneous speech datasets are used to study real-world interaction and expressive phenomena [N4-F4]. The SSSD paper describes spontaneous two-party conversations and emphasizes longer conversations averaging 25–30 minutes, which allows study of discourse phenomena over extended periods [N2-F2]. In the synthesis context, spontaneous speech is particularly useful for **prosody-controllable spontaneous TTS** and for synthesizing expressive phenomena such as creaky voice [N4-F4]. The evidence also indicates that spontaneous speech is used to train systems that can handle reduced articulation, fillers, repetitions, and other disfluencies, which are common in natural speech but less present in read speech [N4-F4]. This makes spontaneous data especially relevant for **dialogue systems, speech synthesis, and speech recognition**, where the goal is to model naturally occurring speech rather than highly controlled read speech [N2-F2].

### How each data type supports different synthesis goals
Simulated data support **controllability and reproducibility**, while spontaneous data support **ecological validity and expressive realism**. Simulated data are easier to annotate and manipulate, making them suitable for controllable synthesis tasks such as sketch-conditioned diffusion models, reference-style prompting, and description-based control [N3-F3], [N3-R3]. They are well suited when the priority is **precise prosody/emotion control**. In contrast, spontaneous data are more challenging to annotate because of variability in recording conditions, imbalance in class distributions, and the difficulty of capturing spontaneous affect [N1-F1]. However, spontaneous data are valuable because they capture natural speech phenomena, disfluencies, and conversational pragmatics [N4-F4]. They are better suited when the priority is **realistic, expressive synthesis** that preserves the natural variability of human speech [N3-F3], [N4-F4].

## 4. Prosody and emotion modeling in expressive speech synthesis

Prosody and emotion are modeled in expressive speech synthesis through **controllable features, annotations, and generative models**. The branch report says that prosody is often controlled via sketch-based, reference-based, or description-based signals. DrawSpeech uses prosody sketches drawn by users, which serve as a rough indication of the expected prosody trends, and then recovers detailed pitch and energy contours from those sketches [N3-F3]. Related work also uses reference speech as a prosody prompt and natural language descriptions to control the synthesis process [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that prosody modeling remains a persistent challenge in advanced natural language processing systems, and that expressive TTS aims to control tone, emotion, and voice style through nonverbal tags like (laughs) or (gasps) [N6-R2]. This indicates that prosody modeling in synthesis is not only about pitch and energy but also about emotional tone and stylistic cues.

For emotion and prosody control, the data needed are **prosody sketches, reference speech, description prompts, or emotion tags**. DrawSpeech requires a sketch of the desired prosody [N3-F3]. The same synthesis paper also notes that reference speech can be used as a prosody prompt, and that description-based guidance can specify the desired prosody [N3-F3]. In the broader context, emotion modeling in expressive speech synthesis depends on data that capture emotional prosody, affective cues, and speaker tone, as well as the ability to associate these with the speech signal [N6-R2]. The evidence also indicates that spontaneous speech datasets are useful for emotion and prosody because they contain natural, ecologically valid expressive phenomena [N4-F4].

The models differ across simulated and spontaneous data in how they are trained and what they can learn. Simulated data are easier to annotate and manipulate, making them suitable for controllable synthesis tasks such as sketch-conditioned diffusion models, reference-style prompting, and description-based control [N3-F3], [N3-R3]. The evidence suggests that simulated data can be generated in large quantities and are often used to train systems that prioritize **controllability** and **fine-grained prosody/emotion control** [N3-R2], [N5-R1]. In contrast, spontaneous data are more challenging to annotate because of variability in recording conditions, imbalance in class distributions, and the difficulty of capturing spontaneous affect [N1-F1]. However, spontaneous data are valuable for modeling natural prosody and emotion because they contain disfluencies, fillers, repetitions, and other conversational phenomena that are not easily replicated in read speech [N4-F4]. The result is that simulated data are used when the goal is **precise controllability**, while spontaneous data are used when the goal is **realistic, expressive synthesis** that preserves the natural variability of human speech [N3-F3], [N4-F4], [N5-R1].

---

## 5. Summary of tradeoffs

The branch reports collectively show a clear tradeoff between **simulated** and **spontaneous expressive speech data**:

- **Simulated data** are easier to collect, manipulate, and annotate, and they support **precise prosody and emotion control**. They are well suited for controllable synthesis, zero-shot style control, and systems like DrawSpeech [N3-F3], [N3-R2], [N5-R1].
- **Spontaneous data** are harder to collect and annotate, but they capture **natural prosody, emotion, and conversational phenomena**. They are better suited for modeling **ecologically valid, expressive speech** and for tasks such as prosody-controllable spontaneous TTS [N4-F4], [N2-F2].

In short, simulated data are the workhorse for **controllability**, while spontaneous data are the workhorse for **realism**. The best expressive speech synthesis systems often combine both types of data: simulated data for controlled synthesis and spontaneous data for ecological validity [N3-R3], [N4-F4], [N5-R1].
